newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPs flex new investigative muscles.
newsitem.headline: MEPs flex new investigative muscles.

text.p: The European Parliament's temporary committee of inquiry into mad cow disease, which begins work on Tuesday, is the second example of MEPs wielding a new power accorded them by the Maastricht treaty.

Article 138c of the treaty allows the parliament to set up a committee to investigate alleged violations or maladministration of European Union law by an EU institution or body, a member state administration or a person mandated by the Union to apply EU law.

A committee of inquiry can only be set up if it has the backing of at least a quarter of the parliament's 626 members and must include at least one representative from each of the assembly's nine political groups.
It has powers of inquiry similar to those of the EU's judicial bodies but it cannot investigate matters that are already being dealt with by EU or national courts.
A committee is given up to one year to complete its work and report back to the parliament, although MEPs can agree to extend the deadline for two further three-month periods.

The parliament set up its first committee of inquiry on December 13, 1995 to look into alleged fraud in the EU's transit system, which the European Court of Auditors says is cheating the EU budget of nearly 200 million ecus a year.

That committee, chaired by British Socialist John Tomlinson, has 12 months to complete its task of interviewing officials from the EU and the member states, the International Road Transport Union, customs officers, road hauliers and other witnesses.
It may request a further three months to complete its recommendations, parliamentary officials said.
The 19-member committee of inquiry into BSE (bovine spongiform encepalopathy) was formed on July 17, 1996.

It has until November 17 to consider whether the European Commission and certain member states failed correctly to inform the public about BSE, monitor the ban on British beef exports or adopt adequate measures for protecting public health and restoring the smooth operation of the beef market.

Committee chairman Manuel Medina, a Spanish Socialist and an expert in international law, said in July he intended to summon government ministers, which would be the first time ministers had been called to appear before an EU public inquiry.
